title: Risk averse fractional trading using the current drawdown

items.abstract: <jats:p>Maximum drawdown is among the most critical risk metrics, since other strategy deficiencies ultimately translate into capital loss and manifest as drawdown. Using drawdown as an illustrative case, this study presents an experimental proof of concept of quantum computing for risk assessment of trading algorithm performance. The probability that maximum drawdown exceeds 5% over eight trades (win rate 0.4054, reward-to-risk 1.92, 2% risk per trade) is estimated. Maximum likelihood amplitude estimation with a 15-qubit circuit on a noiseless Qiskit Aer simulator yields 59.257%, versus 59.324% by exact enumeration (absolute error 0.067 percentage points) and 59.310% by 200,000-path Monte Carlo. The code for this paper is available on GitHub.</jats:p>
title: Proof-of-Concept Risk Assessment of Trading Algorithm Performance with Quantum Amplitude Estimation, Focused on Maximum Drawdown

title: Risk Metrics in Leverage Space and Drawdown

items.abstract: <jats:p>While banks’ proprietary trading can be essential to a range of key banking services, it may also involve socially useless “gambling” aimed at exploiting the safety net. As gambling opportunities become more lucrative, banks find it increasingly costly to allocate scarce resources to lending and not to gambling. To induce banks to lend, loan rates must rise, thus stifling real economic activity. Eventually, gambling crowds out lending and, with it, socially useful trading that complements lending. Ring-fencing banks’ core banking businesses makes gambling in securities markets less lucrative, but it can also spur even more destructive gambling in loan markets.</jats:p>
title: Proprietary Trading and the Real Economy

items.abstract: <jats:p>The evaluations sold by proprietary trading firms are contracts with a bounded premium, a contingent payoff and termination by an absorbing event defined on the drawdown of the P&amp;L. This paper derives their success probability in closed form as a chain of first-passage problems, with six contractual parameters: profit target, drawdown buffer, the level at which the barrier stops trailing, the frequency at which it is updated, the frequency at which breach is checked, and the daily loss limit. The expression reproduces simulation with an error below 1% within its range of validity, which is stated. Applied to thirteen products of the same account size collected from official sources, the success probability varies by 62% across products that advertise identical profit target and drawdown buffer. The variation comes entirely from parameters that the firms publish but not alongside the price, and that no industry comparison records. Two criteria assessable from published terms follow from the valuation: the minimum productivity that makes an evaluation worth its price, and a sufficient condition under which it is not worth it to any buyer. Carried into the unit P&amp;L, both converge on a single figure-the break-even conversion rate-which is simultaneously the buyer's viability threshold and the point at which the seller's contribution vanishes. The pass rates the industry publishes lie below it; the one the model predicts, above. The difference implies a drift for the average buyer three to thirty times larger than any plausible execution cost, and places the origin of the margin not in the price of the contract but in the selection the evaluation performs.</jats:p>
title: <p>Valuing Proprietary Trading Firm Evaluation Contracts: Closed Form, Cross-Firm Dispersion and the Source of the Margin</p>
